description: This topic examines how independent African governments, especially Tanzania, struggled to expand education, health, water, sanitation and housing services to overcome the inherited colonial legacy of limited, unequal and racially based social provision.

mcq.questionText: What was the main characteristic of social services in Tanganyika at the time of independence in 1961?

options.text: They were free, plentiful and equally shared among all races
They were limited, unequally distributed and organised along racial lines
They were fully controlled by African co-operative societies
They were provided mainly by the United Nations

mcq.explanation: Under colonial rule social services such as schools and hospitals were few, concentrated in towns and divided by race, with Europeans and Asians receiving far better services than Africans.

mcq.questionText: Which three 'enemies' did Mwalimu Julius Nyerere identify as the main targets of social service provision after independence?
mcq.explanation: Nyerere declared that the new nation had to fight the three enemies of poverty, ignorance and disease, which justified the rapid expansion of education, health and other social services.

mcq.questionText: The 1967 policy of Education for Self-Reliance in Tanzania was contained in which document?
mcq.explanation: Education for Self-Reliance was a key part of the policy of Socialism and Self-Reliance announced in the Arusha Declaration of 1967.

mcq.questionText: What was the chief aim of the policy of Education for Self-Reliance (ESR)?

options.text: To prepare students mainly for white-collar jobs in the towns
To link education with productive work and the needs of the rural community
To send all secondary students abroad for further study
To keep education in the hands of religious missions

mcq.explanation: ESR sought to remove the colonial bias of education by relating learning to manual work, self-reliance and rural development rather than to elitist office employment.

mcq.questionText: Which mass campaign greatly raised the number of Tanzanians who could read and write during the 1970s?
mcq.explanation: Tanzania launched large adult and mass literacy campaigns in the 1970s that dramatically reduced illiteracy and were praised by UNESCO as among the most successful in Africa.

mcq.questionText: Universal Primary Education (UPE) in Tanzania aimed to achieve what?

options.text: Free university education for all citizens
Enrolment of every child of school-going age in primary school
Education only for children of party members
Compulsory military training for all pupils

mcq.explanation: UPE was the goal of providing primary education to all children of the right age, leading to a massive building of schools and training of teachers from the mid-1970s.

mcq.questionText: In Kenya, what name was given to the spirit of community self-help that built many schools and clinics after independence?
mcq.explanation: Harambee, a Swahili word meaning 'let us pull together', was the self-help spirit that mobilised communities in Kenya to build schools, dispensaries and other facilities.

mcq.questionText: What does Primary Health Care emphasise as the foundation of a national health system?

options.text: Expensive specialist treatment in large city hospitals
Basic, accessible health services close to the people, including prevention
Sending all patients overseas for treatment

mcq.explanation: Primary Health Care focuses on affordable, accessible preventive and basic curative services such as dispensaries, immunisation and health education for the majority.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following best describes a major preventive health measure expanded after independence?

options.text: Mass immunisation of children against diseases such as measles and polio

mcq.explanation: Independent governments expanded immunisation programmes to protect children from killer diseases, a cheap and effective way of fighting disease.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following was a common challenge to expanding social services in newly independent African states?

options.text: Too many trained doctors and teachers
Shortage of funds, trained staff and rapid population growth
A shrinking population needing fewer services

mcq.explanation: Limited budgets, few trained personnel and a fast-growing population made it very difficult to provide enough good-quality services for everyone.

mcq.questionText: The policy of 'cost sharing' introduced in social services from the late 1980s and 1990s meant that:

options.text: Users had to contribute fees towards the cost of services such as health and education
Services were given only to the rich

mcq.explanation: Under economic reforms and structural adjustment, governments introduced cost sharing so that beneficiaries paid part of the cost, easing pressure on strained state budgets.

mcq.questionText: Which approach allows private companies, religious bodies and the state to work together in providing social services in recent years?
mcq.explanation: Public-Private Partnership encourages co-operation between government and private or voluntary providers to widen access to education, health and other services.

mcq.questionText: A major imbalance in the distribution of social services in independent Tanzania was between:

options.text: Lake zone and the ocean only

mcq.explanation: Despite efforts to spread services, towns continued to enjoy better schools, hospitals and water than rural areas, creating a persistent rural-urban imbalance.

mcq.questionText: Clean and safe water supply was promoted after independence mainly because it helps to:

options.text: Increase the price of farm crops
Prevent water-borne diseases and improve public health
End the need for hospitals altogether

mcq.explanation: Providing clean water and good sanitation reduces diseases such as cholera, dysentery and typhoid, directly supporting the fight against disease.

mcq.questionText: Which statement best explains the role of donors in social service provision in many African countries?

options.text: Donors completely replaced national governments in all services
Donors provided funds, expertise and projects that supplemented government efforts but also created dependency
Donors only built houses for ministers
Donors refused to support education and health

mcq.explanation: Foreign donors and agencies financed many schools, hospitals and water schemes, but heavy reliance on them created a problem of dependency on external aid.

fib.questionText: At independence, colonial social services in Tanganyika were organised along _____ lines, giving Europeans and Asians better access than Africans.
fib.explanation: Colonial education and health services were divided by race, with the best facilities reserved for Europeans and Asians.

fib.questionText: The three enemies that Nyerere said the nation must fight were poverty, ignorance and _____.
fib.explanation: Poverty, ignorance and disease were named as the three enemies that social services were meant to overcome.

fib.questionText: The policy of Education for _____ was introduced in 1967 to relate learning to productive work and rural development.
fib.explanation: Education for Self-Reliance aimed to make education practical and linked to the needs of the community.

fib.questionText: The goal of enrolling every child of school-going age in primary school was known by the abbreviation _____.
fib.explanation: UPE stands for Universal Primary Education, the campaign to give primary schooling to all eligible children.

fib.questionText: Large national _____ campaigns in the 1970s taught many Tanzanian adults to read and write.
fib.explanation: Adult and mass literacy campaigns greatly reduced illiteracy among Tanzanian adults.

fib.questionText: In Kenya, the spirit of community self-help used to build schools and clinics was called _____.
fib.explanation: Harambee means 'let us pull together' and described community fundraising and self-help projects.

fib.questionText: The approach that stresses basic, accessible and preventive health services close to the people is called Primary _____ Care.
fib.explanation: Primary Health Care emphasises affordable, accessible and preventive services for the majority.

fib.questionText: The policy requiring users to pay part of the cost of services such as health and education is known as _____ sharing.
fib.explanation: Cost sharing was introduced during economic reforms so beneficiaries contributed to the cost of services.

fib.questionText: A persistent inequality in service distribution was the imbalance between rural and _____ areas.
fib.explanation: Towns continued to receive better services than the countryside, producing a rural-urban imbalance.

fib.questionText: Heavy reliance on foreign aid for social services created a problem of _____ on donors.
fib.explanation: Depending too much on donor funding made services vulnerable, a problem known as dependency.

tf.questionText: At independence, social services in Tanganyika were widely available and equally shared among all people.
tf.explanation: Colonial services were limited, urban-based and divided by race, not equally shared.

tf.questionText: Nyerere identified poverty, ignorance and disease as the three enemies the nation had to fight.
tf.explanation: These three enemies were the main justification for expanding social services after independence.

tf.questionText: Education for Self-Reliance encouraged students to despise manual work and seek only office jobs.
tf.explanation: ESR did the opposite: it valued manual work and linked education to production and rural life.

tf.questionText: Universal Primary Education led to a large increase in the building of primary schools and training of teachers.
tf.explanation: To enrol all children, the government built many schools and trained large numbers of teachers.

tf.questionText: Tanzania's adult literacy campaigns of the 1970s were considered a failure by international bodies such as UNESCO.
tf.explanation: The campaigns were praised by UNESCO as among the most successful in Africa for sharply reducing illiteracy.

tf.questionText: Immunisation of children was expanded after independence as a cheap and effective way of fighting disease.
tf.explanation: Mass immunisation protected children from killer diseases and was a key preventive measure.

tf.questionText: Providing clean water and good sanitation has no effect on the spread of disease.
tf.explanation: Clean water and sanitation greatly reduce water-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid.

tf.questionText: Rapid population growth made it harder for governments to provide enough social services.
tf.explanation: A fast-growing population increased demand faster than services could be built, straining provision.

tf.questionText: Cost sharing means that all social services were made completely free of charge.
tf.explanation: Cost sharing required users to pay part of the cost, not to receive everything free.

tf.questionText: Public-Private Partnership allows the government and private or voluntary bodies to co-operate in providing services.
tf.explanation: PPP combines state and private/voluntary effort to widen access to education, health and other services.

summary.questionText: Describe the state of social services in Tanganyika at the time of independence.
summary.correctAnswer: At independence social services were limited in number, concentrated mainly in urban areas and distributed unequally along racial lines, with Europeans and Asians receiving far better education and health services than the African majority, many of whom in rural areas had little or no access at all.
summary.explanation: This shows the colonial legacy of scarce, urban-biased and racially divided services that the new government inherited.

summary.questionText: Explain what is meant by the 'three enemies' and how they shaped social service provision.
summary.correctAnswer: The three enemies were poverty, ignorance and disease. To fight ignorance the government expanded education and literacy; to fight disease it built dispensaries and hospitals and ran immunisation; and to fight poverty it promoted development and self-reliance, so the three enemies became the guiding goals of social service expansion.
summary.explanation: It links the slogan directly to the expansion of education, health and development services.

summary.questionText: Outline the main features of the policy of Education for Self-Reliance (1967).
summary.correctAnswer: Education for Self-Reliance aimed to remove the colonial, elitist bias of education by relating learning to productive work, making schools partly self-supporting through farming and projects, stressing co-operation and equality rather than competition, and preparing learners to serve and develop the rural community instead of seeking only white-collar town jobs.
summary.explanation: It captures ESR's emphasis on practical, communal and rural-oriented education.

summary.questionText: Describe the efforts made to expand education after independence in Tanzania.
summary.correctAnswer: The government built many more primary and secondary schools, trained large numbers of teachers, removed racial barriers, launched Universal Primary Education to enrol all children, ran national adult and mass literacy campaigns that greatly reduced illiteracy, and at times offered free or subsidised education to widen access.
summary.explanation: It lists the key educational measures: more schools, teachers, UPE, literacy and free education.

summary.questionText: Explain the measures taken to improve health services after independence.
summary.correctAnswer: Governments built dispensaries, health centres and hospitals closer to the people, trained more nurses and medical staff, adopted Primary Health Care emphasising prevention, expanded immunisation against killer diseases, provided maternal and child health services, and ran campaigns against major diseases as part of fighting the enemy of disease.
summary.explanation: It covers facilities, staff, primary health care, immunisation and disease campaigns.

summary.questionText: Discuss the importance of water supply and sanitation among social services.
summary.correctAnswer: After independence governments and communities sank wells, built water schemes and piped supplies, and promoted latrines and clean surroundings, because safe water and good sanitation reduce water-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid, save the time spent fetching water, and improve the health and productivity of the population.
summary.explanation: It connects water and sanitation projects to disease prevention and improved welfare.

summary.questionText: Explain the role of communities and self-help in providing social services.
summary.correctAnswer: Communities contributed labour, materials and money through self-help schemes such as Harambee in Kenya and nation-building or Ujamaa efforts in Tanzania, building schools, dispensaries, roads and water points themselves; this reduced the burden on government, encouraged unity and self-reliance, and made services available where state funds alone were not enough.
summary.explanation: It highlights community participation through Harambee and self-help as a key source of services.

summary.questionText: Identify the achievements of social service provision since independence.
summary.correctAnswer: Achievements include the removal of racial barriers, a great rise in literacy through UPE and adult campaigns, many more schools, dispensaries and hospitals, wider immunisation and longer life expectancy, increased access to clean water, and a stronger sense of equality and national unity compared with the colonial period.
summary.explanation: It summarises the positive results in education, health, water and equality.

summary.questionText: Explain the major challenges faced in providing social services after independence.
summary.correctAnswer: The main challenges were shortage of funds and a weak economy, too few trained teachers, doctors and other staff, rapid population growth that outpaced service expansion, rural-urban imbalance, declining quality of overstretched services, and heavy dependence on foreign donors and loans.
summary.explanation: It lists funding, staffing, population, imbalance, quality and dependency problems.

summary.questionText: Describe the recent reforms introduced in social service provision.
summary.correctAnswer: From the late 1980s and 1990s, economic reforms introduced cost sharing so that users contributed to the cost of health and education, encouraged Public-Private Partnership and private and religious providers, decentralised services to local government, and sought greater community participation in order to ease the burden on the state and improve efficiency.
summary.explanation: It covers cost sharing, PPP, private providers and decentralisation as the main recent reforms.

hoq.questionText: Why might the rapid expansion of Universal Primary Education in the mid-1970s have led to complaints about a fall in the quality of education?

options.text: Because enrolment grew faster than the supply of trained teachers, classrooms and learning materials
Because there were too few children to fill the new schools
Because the government refused to build any new schools
Because all teaching was carried out by foreign donors

hoq.explanation: Pushing all children into school quickly meant overcrowded classes, untrained teachers and shortages of books, so quantity rose faster than quality could be maintained.

hoq.questionText: Which argument best explains why heavy dependence on foreign donors for social services can be a weakness for an independent state?

options.text: Donors always give money without any conditions
Services may collapse or be redirected if donor priorities or aid change, reducing genuine self-reliance
Donor funding makes a country fully independent of all outside influence
Donor projects can never be linked to political conditions

hoq.explanation: Relying on aid means services depend on the goodwill and priorities of others; if aid is cut or tied to conditions, programmes suffer, contradicting the goal of self-reliance.

hoq.questionText: Evaluate why the introduction of cost sharing in the 1990s was controversial as a way of solving the funding problem in social services.

options.text: Because it raised more money but risked excluding the poor who could not afford the fees
Because it made all services completely free for everyone
Because it removed the need for any government spending
Because it applied only to rich urban residents

hoq.explanation: Cost sharing eased pressure on the budget and improved supplies, but charging fees could lock out poor and rural people, working against the goal of equal access to services.
